questions.prompt: A symmetric matrix \(A\) is positive definite when
questions.explanation: Positive definite means the quadratic form is positive on every nonzero vector. In dimension 2, \(\det A > 0\) also holds for a negative definite matrix. Positive entries and a positive trace do not rule out a negative eigenvalue.

questions.explanation: The form is \(2\cdot 1^2 + 8\cdot 1^2 = 10\). Either diagonal entry alone would give 2 or 8. The Euclidean squared length of \((1,1)\) is 2, which ignores the matrix.

questions.prompt: For a symmetric matrix, the eigenvalue test says the matrix is positive definite exactly when
questions.explanation: The quadratic form is a sum of \(\lambda_i y_i^2\) in the eigenbasis, so it stays positive for every nonzero vector exactly when every \(\lambda_i\) is positive. One positive eigenvalue is not enough. A zero eigenvalue makes the form only semidefinite.

options: at least one eigenvalue is positive
the matrix has a zero eigenvalue

questions.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 3 = (\lambda-3)(\lambda+1)\). The eigenvalues are 3 and \(-1\), so the form takes both signs. A positive trace or a positive diagonal does not prevent the negative eigenvalue.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>symmetric matrix with a large off-diagonal entry</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A symmetric 2 by 2 matrix whose off-diagonal entries exceed the diagonal.
options: positive definite, because the trace is positive
positive semidefinite, because the diagonal entries are positive
indefinite, because its eigenvalues have opposite signs
negative definite, because the off-diagonal entries are the larger ones

questions.prompt: What is the smaller eigenvalue of \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)?
questions.explanation: The roots of \(\lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 3 = 0\) are 3 and \(-1\). The smaller one is \(-1\). The trace 2 is their sum, and the diagonal entry 1 is neither eigenvalue.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>symmetric matrix with a large off-diagonal entry</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A symmetric 2 by 2 matrix whose off-diagonal entries exceed the diagonal.

questions.explanation: \(\det = 1 - 4 = -3\), the product of the eigenvalues 3 and \(-1\). The trace is 2. A positive determinant would have required both eigenvalues to share a sign.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>symmetric matrix with a large off-diagonal entry</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A symmetric 2 by 2 matrix whose off-diagonal entries exceed the diagonal.

questions.prompt: If \(A\) is symmetric positive definite, a level set \(x^T A x = c\) with \(c > 0\) is
questions.explanation: In the eigenbasis the equation is a sum of \(\lambda_i y_i^2 = c\) with every \(\lambda_i > 0\), which is an ellipsoid. Opposite signs would give a hyperbola. A zero eigenvalue would drop a square term and flatten the set.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>axis-aligned ellipse</title><line x1="28" y1="104" x2="256" y2="104"/><polygon points="256,104 249.6,106.7 249.6,101.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="120" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="104" rx="86" ry="46"/><line x1="54" y1="104" x2="226" y2="104" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="140" y1="58" x2="140" y2="150" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: An axis-aligned ellipse, longer along the first axis.
options: a hyperbola opening along an eigenvector
a pair of lines through the origin
a square aligned with the coordinate axes
an ellipse whose axes lie along the eigenvectors

questions.prompt: The level set \(2 x_1^2 + 8 x_2^2 = 8\) is an ellipse. What is its semi-axis length along \(x_1\)?
questions.explanation: Divide by 8 to get \(x_1^2/4 + x_2^2/1 = 1\). The semi-axis along \(x_1\) is 2, and the one along \(x_2\) is 1. Swapping them uses the coefficient 8 as if it were the squared length.

questions.explanation: \(x^T A x = x_1^2 = 9\). The second coordinate is multiplied by the zero eigenvalue, which is why the form can vanish for a nonzero vector. The squared Euclidean length \(9+16 = 25\) would be the form of the identity, not of this \(A\).

questions.prompt: A quadratic \(f(x) = \frac12 x^T A x\) with symmetric \(A\) is convex when \(A\) is positive semidefinite. For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), what is the smallest eigenvalue?
questions.explanation: A diagonal matrix lists its eigenvalues on the diagonal. The smaller one is 4, and both are positive, so \(A\) is positive definite and the quadratic is strictly convex. The trace 13 is the sum, not the smaller eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: If \(D\) is symmetric positive definite and \(g \ne 0\), the direction \(d = -D g\) satisfies
questions.explanation: \(g^T d = -g^T D g < 0\) because \(D\) is positive definite and \(g \ne 0\). That negative directional derivative is what makes \(d\) a descent direction. Orthogonality would give 0, and \(Dd = 0\) would say \(d\) is a null vector.

questions.prompt: The pairing \(\langle u, v \rangle = u^T A v\) is an inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) when the symmetric matrix \(A\) is
questions.explanation: An inner product must give \(\langle u, u \rangle > 0\) for every \(u \ne 0\), which is positive definiteness of \(A\). A singular or indefinite matrix makes the square zero or negative for some nonzero vector. A negative semidefinite matrix reverses the sign.
